subject: Geography
description: Covers Venus greenhouse effect, Asteroid belt, Mars, Uranus tilt, and Ganymede.

questions.stem: Which planet in our solar system has the highest surface temperature, despite not being the closest planet to the Sun?

options.option_text: Venus
Mercury
Mars
Jupiter

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Venus is the second planet from the Sun, but it is much hotter than Mercury (the closest planet). Venus has an extremely thick atmosphere composed of 96% carbon dioxide, topped with clouds of sulfuric acid. This creates a runaway greenhouse effect, trapping the sun's heat. The surface temperature on Venus averages a scorching 465°C (867°F), hot enough to melt lead.
DECOY BUSTING: Mercury is closest to the sun, but it has virtually no atmosphere to trap heat. So while its day side is 430°C, its night side drops to a freezing -180°C. Mars is much further out and has a very thin, cold atmosphere. Jupiter is a freezing gas giant.
EXAM INSIGHT: Venus is also unique because it has retrograde rotation—it spins on its axis in the opposite direction of most planets (including Earth). On Venus, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

questions.stem: The asteroid belt, a torus-shaped region in the Solar System containing millions of rocky bodies, is located between the orbits of which two planets?

options.option_text: Mars and Jupiter
Earth and Mars
Jupiter and Saturn
Venus and Earth

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The main asteroid belt is located roughly between the orbits of Mars (the last terrestrial planet) and Jupiter (the first gas giant). It is believed to be remnants from the early solar system that failed to coalesce into a planet, primarily due to the immense gravitational disruptions caused by massive Jupiter.
DECOY BUSTING: There are asteroids that cross Earth's orbit (Near-Earth Asteroids), but the main belt is strictly between Mars and Jupiter. The Kuiper Belt is another ring of icy bodies, but it is located far beyond Neptune at the edge of the solar system.
EXAM INSIGHT: The largest object in the asteroid belt is Ceres, which is so massive (about 940 km across) that its own gravity has pulled it into a spherical shape, classifying it as a "Dwarf Planet" (like Pluto).

questions.stem: Which planet is known as the 'Red Planet' due to the widespread presence of iron oxide on its surface?

options.option_text: Mars
Jupiter
Saturn
Uranus

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Mars appears red because its surface is covered in fine dust containing iron(III) oxide (commonly known as rust). This dust gets kicked up into the thin Martian atmosphere by massive dust storms, giving the entire planet a reddish hue when viewed from Earth.
DECOY BUSTING: Jupiter is banded with orange/white clouds of ammonia. Saturn is pale yellow. Uranus is pale blue due to methane in its atmosphere.
EXAM INSIGHT: Mars hosts Olympus Mons, the largest volcano and highest known mountain in the entire solar system (nearly three times the height of Mount Everest). It also has two small, irregularly shaped moons named Phobos and Deimos.

questions.stem: Which of the following planets rotates on its axis at such an extreme tilt (about 98 degrees) that it appears to roll on its side as it orbits the Sun?

options.option_text: Uranus
Neptune
Saturn
Venus

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Uranus has a highly unusual axial tilt of 97.77 degrees. While Earth is tilted at a mild 23.5 degrees (which gives us our seasons), Uranus is essentially knocked over on its side. Astronomers believe a catastrophic collision with an Earth-sized protoplanet early in the solar system's history caused this extreme tilt. 
DECOY BUSTING: Venus spins backwards, but it is mostly upright. Saturn is famous for its rings but has a normal tilt. Neptune is Uranus's twin in composition, but its tilt is a normal 28 degrees.
EXAM INSIGHT: Because of this extreme tilt, the poles of Uranus experience 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by 42 years of continuous darkness during its 84-year orbit around the Sun.

questions.stem: Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System (even larger than the planet Mercury), orbits which planet?

options.option_text: Jupiter
Saturn
Uranus
Neptune

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Ganymede is the largest and most massive moon in the solar system. It orbits Jupiter and is the only moon in the solar system known to have its own magnetic field. 
DECOY BUSTING: Saturn's largest moon is Titan (the second largest in the solar system and the only moon with a thick, Earth-like nitrogen atmosphere). Uranus's largest moon is Titania. Neptune's largest moon is Triton (famous for orbiting backward/retrograde).
EXAM INSIGHT: Ganymede is one of the four "Galilean moons" of Jupiter, discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 using his newly invented telescope. The other three are Io (most volcanically active body in the solar system), Europa (has a massive subsurface ocean), and Callisto.

questions.stem: Which planet is often called Earth's 'twin planet' because of its nearly identical size, mass, and internal rocky composition?

options.option_text: Mars, the fourth planet with a thin reddish atmosphere
Venus, the second planet with diameter roughly 95% of Earth's
Neptune, an ice giant with a slightly larger equatorial radius
Mercury, the innermost and smallest rocky planet of the System

questions.explanation: Venus has a diameter of ~12,104 km (Earth's is ~12,742 km) and a mass ~81.5% of Earth's, earning the 'twin' label. Mars is a common distractor but has only ~53% of Earth's diameter and just ~10.7% of Earth's mass, making it far smaller.

questions.stem: Following the IAU's 2006 resolution that reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet, which is now the smallest among the eight recognised planets of the Solar System?

options.option_text: Mars, the fourth planet with a mean radius of 3,390 km
Venus, the second planet with diameter close to Earth's
Mercury, the innermost planet with a mean radius of 2,440 km
Saturn, the sixth planet renowned for its prominent ring system

questions.explanation: Mercury, with a mean radius of ~2,440 km, is the smallest of the eight planets since Pluto's reclassification in 2006. Before 2006 Pluto held that title, so many candidates still confuse this; Mercury is now definitively the smallest recognised planet.

questions.stem: Olympus Mons on Mars stands ~22 km tall — three times the height of Everest. Which of the following best explains why such enormous volcanoes can form on Mars but not on Earth?

options.option_text: Mars has stronger surface gravity, compressing volcanic material
Mars lacks tectonic plate movement, letting lava accumulate in one spot
Mars has a thinner crust allowing greater volumes of magma to escape
Mars lies closer to the asteroid belt, increasing volcanic frequency

questions.explanation: On Earth, moving tectonic plates carry crust over mantle hotspots, producing chains of smaller volcanoes (e.g., Hawaiian islands). Mars has a single, stationary lithospheric plate, so the hotspot feeds one location for billions of years, piling lava to extreme heights. The stronger-gravity option is wrong — Mars's gravity is only ~0.38 g, weaker than Earth's.

questions.stem: Apart from Uranus, which other planet in the Solar System rotates in a retrograde direction — opposite to the orbital motion of most planets — causing the Sun to rise in the west on its surface?

options.option_text: Mercury, the planet nearest to the Sun in its orbital path
Mars, the fourth planet orbited by Phobos and Deimos
Venus, the second planet where the Sun rises in the west
Neptune, the outermost planet with supersonic wind speeds

questions.explanation: Venus rotates east-to-west (retrograde), the opposite of Earth, so a Venusian observer would see sunrise in the west and sunset in the east. Mercury is the classic distractor — it spins extremely slowly but still prograde (west-to-east). Uranus has near-90° axial tilt rather than a true retrograde spin.

questions.stem: The Cassini-Huygens mission successfully deployed the Huygens probe onto the surface of Titan in January 2005, the first landing on a moon in the outer Solar System. Titan is a natural satellite of which planet?

options.option_text: Jupiter, explored earlier by the Galileo and Juno spacecraft
Uranus, the ice giant tilted at an extreme 98-degree axis
Saturn, whose moon Titan has a dense nitrogen-rich atmosphere
Neptune, whose largest moon Triton orbits in a retrograde path

questions.explanation: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the second-largest moon in the Solar System (after Ganymede). It has a dense nitrogen atmosphere (~1.45 times Earth's surface pressure) and hydrocarbon lakes. Jupiter is a common distractor because it too has been explored by dedicated orbiters (Galileo, Juno), but Cassini-Huygens was exclusively a Saturn system mission.

questions.stem: In solar-system formation theory, the 'frost line' at roughly 2.7 AU from the Sun is a critical threshold. Which statement best explains why planets that formed beyond this line are predominantly gas giants or ice giants?

options.option_text: Solar wind strips volatile gases near the Sun, leaving only rocky cores
Solid icy grains form beyond 2.7 AU, giving cores enough mass to capture gas
Rocky silicate material becomes completely absent beyond this boundary
Jupiter's gravity scatters all rocky planetesimals beyond 2.7 AU outward

questions.explanation: Beyond the frost line, volatile compounds (water, ammonia, methane) solidify into ice grains. This dramatically increases the density of solid material available to protoplanets, allowing cores to grow massive enough (~10 Earth masses) to gravitationally capture hydrogen and helium gas, forming gas/ice giants. Option D describes Jupiter's role in the asteroid belt gap (Kirkwood gaps), not the frost line mechanism itself.

questions.stem: Jupiter's moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede are locked in the 'Laplace resonance' — a 1:2:4 orbital resonance. What does this precisely mean?

options.option_text: The three moons orbit Jupiter with exactly the same orbital period
For every orbit of Ganymede, Europa completes two and Io four orbits
The three moons align in a perfect straight line every fourth orbit
Each moon's orbital period increases by a fixed constant in days

questions.explanation: In Laplace resonance, the orbital periods of Io (~1.77 days), Europa (~3.55 days), and Ganymede (~7.15 days) are in the ratio 4:2:1. So in the time Ganymede completes one orbit, Europa completes exactly two and Io exactly four. Option A (same period) describes co-orbital bodies, not resonance. Option C describes syzygy, a separate gravitational phenomenon.
